title: These startups are chasing the next big thing in LLMs
gist: Four startups are attacking the transformer's quadratic dense-attention bottleneck from different angles: Subquadratic (sparse attention), Manifest AI (power retention), Liquid AI (hybrid liquid foundation models 4x smaller than rivals), Inception (diffusion LLMs claiming 10x speed at GPT-4-2023 quality) and Pathway (state-space Dragon Hatchling, which solved 97% of a 250,000-puzzle sudoku benchmark that top LLMs failed entirely). The framing is that reasoning models and long context are workarounds for transformer flaws, making architecture succession a live risk to the $50B-per-lab compute and data-center power demand trajectory.

insights.claim: Dense attention requires comparing every token with every other token, so a 10,000-word document can force a transformer into roughly 50 million multiplications, which is the primary driver of LLM power consumption.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Quantifies why inference cost scales super-linearly with context length: any architecture that breaks this quadratic term directly attacks the largest line item in AI compute budgets.
insights.quote: A document 10,000 words long might require a transformer to perform 50 million multiplications.
insights.locator: Strength in numbers

insights.claim: OpenAI is set to spend $50 billion on computing in 2026 according to its president Greg Brockman, a figure cited as evidence that transformer inefficiency now carries balance-sheet-scale costs.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A concrete anchor for frontier-lab compute burn; architecture efficiency gains would show up as either margin expansion or a hit to compute-vendor demand.
insights.quote: OpenAI is set to spend $50 billion on computing this year, according to the company’s president, Greg Brockman.
insights.locator: The costs are huge

insights.claim: The International Energy Agency predicts total electricity consumed by data centers will double by 2030, tying LLM architecture choices directly to power demand forecasts.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Utilities, grid and power-generation theses are partly a bet that transformer-style dense attention remains the dominant architecture through 2030; efficiency breakthroughs are the bear case.
insights.quote: the total amount of electricity consumed by data centers will double by 2030
insights.locator: And the International Energy Agency predicts

insights.claim: Recent headline LLM advances such as reasoning models and long-context handling are framed not as natural extensions of the transformer but as workarounds patching over its fundamental flaws.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Reframes the current capability race as accumulating technical debt rather than durable architectural progress, raising the odds of a disruptive architecture shift.
insights.quote: not neat extensions of that core technology but workarounds that patch over some of its fundamental flaws
insights.locator: Way back in the summer of 2017

insights.claim: Transformers process text word by word, which caps how large a context window can practically get, exactly as agents, whole code bases and chain-of-thought scratch pads demand ever more data be held at once.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: The agent and long-context product roadmap is on a collision course with the base architecture, creating the demand pull for the four alternatives profiled.
insights.quote: As LLMs get bigger and better, transformers have become a bottleneck. The technology’s key strength is now a limitation.
insights.locator: What’s more, transformers struggle

insights.claim: The competitive setup favors challengers because startups attacking the architecture have far less to lose than the incumbents currently leading the model race.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Classic disruption asymmetry: incumbents are financially committed to transformer-optimized stacks, so architecture bets are cheaper to underwrite in early-stage names than in frontier labs.
insights.quote: Some will no doubt fail—but they have everything to play for and far less to lose than the companies at the front of the pack today.
insights.locator: Enter a wave of startups

insights.claim: Miami-based Subquadratic claims the first sparse attention mechanism that rivals top mainstream LLMs on tasks including search and coding, with its SubQ model deciding on the fly which words matter for each input.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: If validated, sparse attention collapses the compute per token for search and coding workloads, the two highest-volume commercial LLM use cases.
insights.quote: Subquadratic says its model, SubQ, works by figuring out on the fly—for each piece of text it is given—which words matter and which don’t.
insights.locator: 01: Rethinking attention

insights.claim: Subquadratic's claim is explicitly flagged as unverified, with industry participants still skeptical, and the company's evidence so far is a waitlist of thousands rather than broad availability.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Treat the sparse-attention breakthrough as an unpriced option, not a fact; the near-term catalyst to watch is a public release and third-party benchmark replication.
insights.quote: It’s a huge claim (and some people in the industry remain skeptical).
insights.locator: It’s a huge claim

insights.claim: San Francisco's Manifest AI replaces attention entirely with 'power retention,' giving the model a rolling summary of its context window in which less relevant information is dropped as new data arrives, so the tracked data never blows up.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A bounded-state architecture makes long-running agents economically viable because cost stops scaling with session length, the key blocker for multi-week agent products.
insights.quote: power retention works by providing the model with a rolling summary of its context window
insights.locator: 02 lead-in: It has developed a mechanism it calls power retention

insights.claim: Manifest AI says an existing transformer can be converted into a power retention model with minimal retraining, demonstrated by turning the open-source coding LLM StarCoder into PowerCoder and by releasing Brumby, which it claims rivals versions of Alibaba's Qwen.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Cheap retrofit rather than pretraining from scratch is the distribution wedge: it means adoption could spread across the open-weights ecosystem without frontier-scale capex.
insights.quote: The company says it is possible to adapt a transformer model into a power retention model with minimal retraining.
insights.locator: The basic principle of retention

insights.claim: Manifest AI positions power retention as the default for data-heavy workloads, citing analysis of hours-long video and agents that stay on task for weeks at a time.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Names the two commercial beachheads where a retention architecture would first displace transformers: long-form video understanding and persistent agents.
insights.quote: from analyzing videos that are hours long to building agents that can stay on task for weeks at a time
insights.locator: Manifest AI wants its power retention tech

insights.claim: Sparse attention and power retention differ in what they discard: sparse models like SubQ drop individual words but keep a rough picture of everything seen, while retention keeps a compressed summary and discards the rest.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A useful diligence lens for evaluating efficient-attention startups: ask what information is thrown away and whether the target workload tolerates that loss.
insights.locator: Attention mechanisms force LLMs to keep track

insights.claim: MIT spinout Liquid AI pairs transformers with liquid neural networks into liquid foundation models that are far smaller and lower-energy than mainstream LLMs, and it already ships models to carmakers including Mercedes that run on in-vehicle chips.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Automotive and embedded inference is a commercial market being served today, independent of the frontier-model race, and it does not depend on data center buildout.
insights.locator: 02: Making models smaller and more flexible

insights.claim: Liquid AI's latest models run on a $50 Raspberry Pi, pushing capable inference onto hobbyist-grade hardware.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A hard datapoint on how far the cost floor of on-device inference has fallen, undermining assumptions that every AI workload must route through cloud GPUs.
insights.quote: Its latest models can run on a Raspberry Pi, a low-powered hobbyist computer that costs $50.
insights.locator: 03 lead: Liquid AI’s models are far smaller

insights.claim: Liquid AI gives its models away free to any organization with annual revenue under $10 million and has accumulated almost 34 million downloads, per CEO Ramin Hasani.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A land-grab distribution strategy with a revenue-gated license; the download figure is the traction metric to track against open-weights rivals.
insights.quote: Its models are available for free to any organization with an annual revenue less than $10 million.
insights.locator: Its models are available for free

insights.claim: Liquid neural networks, inspired by worm brains and extending pre-transformer convolutional networks, let a model adapt its behavior to new information after deployment, whereas a trained transformer's behavior is fixed.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Post-deployment adaptation is a genuine capability gap versus transformers and the core technical differentiator to test in any Liquid AI diligence.
insights.quote: Once a model is trained, its behavior is fixed.
insights.locator: Liquid neural networks were inspired by worm brains

insights.claim: Liquid AI's recent LFMs are hybrids of roughly 20% transformers and 80% liquid neural networks, and they match the performance of rival models four times their size, including versions of Alibaba's Qwen and Google's Gemma.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A 4x parameter-efficiency claim against the leading open-weights baselines; if it holds, per-token serving costs for equivalent quality drop sharply.
insights.quote: Its new models match the performance of rivals four times bigger
insights.locator: A typical LLM is built from a stack of transformers

insights.claim: Liquid AI's 20/80 architecture ratio was discovered not by human researchers but by an in-house AI system that searches combinations of liquid, convolutional and transformer blocks for a performance-efficiency sweet spot, which Hasani calls the company's core technology.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: The real moat claim is the automated architecture-design system rather than any single model, which is the asset to underwrite and the thing rivals must replicate.
insights.quote: It’s the core technology of our company right now
insights.locator: That ratio was hit upon by another AI system

insights.claim: Hasani frames the human brain running an AGI-class system on 20 watts as proof that current architectures are nowhere near the efficiency frontier.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A biological efficiency benchmark implying orders-of-magnitude headroom, which is the bear case for straight-line extrapolation of AI power demand.
insights.quote: Your brain is an AGI system, you know, and it operates with 20 watts of power.
insights.locator: Hasani thinks transformers were just the beginning

insights.claim: Palo Alto-based Inception builds LLMs with diffusion, generating whole sentences or paragraphs in one shot rather than one word at a time, which still uses a big transformer to encode meaning but predicts many tokens simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Diffusion is complementary to, not a replacement for, transformers, so it can ride existing hardware and tooling while cutting serving cost per token.
insights.quote: You’re still using a big transformer model, but you can predict many tokens at the same time
insights.locator: 03: Generating text all at once

insights.claim: Ermon and Stanford colleagues solved the math for text diffusion in 2024, producing a model that matched GPT-2's performance at 10 times the speed, and Inception now claims its Mercury 2 model matches some 2023-era GPT-4 models at 10 times the speed.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A repeatable 10x speed multiple at two capability tiers is the quantitative case for diffusion; the gap to note is that parity is with 2023 GPT-4, not current frontier models.
insights.quote: They trained a diffusion model that matched the performance of GPT-2—an LLM that OpenAI built in 2019—but was 10 times faster.
insights.locator: Ermon is also a researcher at Stanford University

insights.claim: Ermon argues the only things that ultimately matter in LLMs are speed and cost, reducing the competitive metric to intelligence per dollar.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A clean valuation lens for model businesses: differentiation collapses toward cost per unit of capability, which favors architecture efficiency over raw scale.
insights.quote: Ultimately, the currency is going to be intelligence per dollar.
insights.locator: The only things that matter are speed and cost

insights.claim: Google is independently building a prototype diffusion LLM called Diffusion Gemma, which Ermon reads as validation rather than threat.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler entry de-risks the technical approach but compresses the startup's window; watch whether Google productizes diffusion text generation.
insights.quote: Google is also experimenting with this approach and has built a prototype LLM called Diffusion Gemma.
insights.locator: Inception is not the only company betting on diffusion

insights.claim: Adapting diffusion from images to text required solving the absence of intermediate states between discrete tokens, since unlike stepping a blue pixel toward red there is nothing between 'cat' and 'dog.'
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Explains why text diffusion lagged image diffusion by years and why the math itself, not compute, was the barrier to entry.
insights.quote: When you have ‘cat’ and ‘dog,’ there is not really something in between.
insights.locator: The challenge was to take a technology designed for image generation

insights.claim: Palo Alto startup Pathway replaces the transformer's attention mechanism with a mathematical state space that compresses information into abstract representations instead of encoding it word by word, in a model called Dragon Hatchling.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: The most architecturally radical of the four bets: it targets capability gaps rather than cost, so its payoff profile is binary rather than incremental.
insights.locator: 04: Moving beyond words

insights.claim: Dragon Hatchling beat more than 97% of a benchmark of over 250,000 very hard sudoku puzzles while several leading LLMs from top labs solved none of them.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A rare clean example of a task class where frontier LLMs score zero, evidence that scaling transformers does not close every capability gap.
insights.quote: Dragon Hatchling beat more than 97% of the puzzles; several leading LLMs from the top labs failed to solve any.
insights.locator: Its standout result so far

insights.claim: Pathway's core argument is that forcing all reasoning through text is itself the constraint, since problems like sudoku, chess and mathematics are not held in the mind as long sentences.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: If non-linguistic reasoning is a distinct capability axis, benchmark leadership on language tasks becomes a weak proxy for progress toward high-value scientific applications.
insights.quote: The eureka moment that pops up in your brain isn’t necessarily in language. We would argue that if you have to reason in language, you’re somehow constrained.
insights.locator: Think of chess or mathematics

insights.claim: Stamirowska concedes a mainstream LLM could read a sudoku book and write code to solve it, but argues the goal is models with more than book smarts because there is no book for curing cancer.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Frames the real prize as novel discovery rather than retrieval-plus-code, the standard against which AI-for-science claims should be judged.
insights.quote: The hope for AI is not to solve sudoku; it’s to cure cancer. There’s not a book for that.
insights.locator: Stamirowska admits that a mainstream LLM

insights.claim: Stamirowska characterizes the transformer as an engineering convenience that the field stumbled onto and that hardened into a religion, arguing it is naive to assume no further breakthrough will occur.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: The sharpest statement of architecture risk: capital allocated on the assumption of transformer permanence is exposed if a successor emerges.
insights.quote: It started a religion, but it’s silly to think that a breakthrough won’t happen again.
insights.locator: Transformers are an engineering convenience
